indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.2.1: Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Identify and name a variety of everyday materials in their immediate environment

skills.description: Name everyday materials commonly found in the home, school and community
Identify/recognise a named material from a picture or simple description
Say where a given material is commonly found in the immediate environment
Link a simple everyday material to one common use

misconceptions: Metal and plastic are the same thing.
Glass is the same as plastic because both are shiny.
Soil and stone are not materials.
Confusing the name of an object with the name of the material.

questions.stem: Which of these is a material?
hints: A material is used to make things.
questions.explanation: Wood is a material used to make tables, chairs, and doors.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name objects or living things instead of materials.

questions.stem: A bottle of water is usually made from which material?
hints: It is light and can be squeezed.
Water bottles are made from this.
questions.explanation: Plastic is a common material used to make water bottles.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse plastic with glass.

questions.stem: Name one material you can find in your classroom.
questions.explanation: There are many materials in the classroom, such as wood for desks and glass for windows.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name objects like a desk instead of the material.

questions.stem: Which of these is a piece of cloth?
hints: What do you wear to school?
questions.explanation: A school uniform is made of cloth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse objects made of cloth with other objects.

questions.stem: Which material is hard and used to make nails?
questions.explanation: Metal is a hard material used to make nails.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any hard material is metal.

questions.stem: Where do we usually get wood from?
questions.explanation: Wood comes from trees.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wood is dug from the ground.

questions.stem: What is plastic commonly used for?
hints: You can put water in it.
questions.explanation: Plastic is used to make buckets, cups, and many other things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse what a material is with what you do with it.

questions.stem: Which of these is a glass object?
questions.explanation: A windowpane is made of glass.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse transparent plastic with glass.

questions.stem: Where is soil usually found?
hints: It is the dirt on the ground.
questions.explanation: Soil is found on the ground.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think soil is only in farms.

questions.stem: What is cloth used for?
questions.explanation: Cloth is used to make clothes, bags, and curtains.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cloth is only for clothes.

questions.stem: What material is a stone usually made of?
hints: You find it on the ground.
questions.explanation: A stone is a hard material found naturally.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones are made by people.

questions.stem: Look at a ruler. What material is it made of?
questions.explanation: Rulers can be made of plastic, wood, or metal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all rulers are plastic.

questions.stem: Why is glass used for windows?
questions.explanation: Glass is used for windows because it is transparent and lets light into a room.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think glass is used because it is pretty.

questions.stem: Why is metal used to make cooking pots?
options: It is hard and can withstand heat
hints: You put pots on a fire.
questions.explanation: Metal is hard and can handle high heat, making it good for cooking pots.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any material can be put on fire.

questions.stem: Kofi has a chair, a bucket, and a shirt. What materials are they made from?
questions.explanation: A chair is often wood, a bucket is plastic, and a shirt is cloth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may mix up the materials for each object.

questions.stem: Name one material found in your kitchen and say what it is used for.

criteria.description: Names a correct material (e.g., metal, plastic, glass)
States a correct use for it

questions.explanation: This tests identifying materials and linking them to uses.

questions.stem: Yaw needs to carry water. Which material is best for making a bucket?
questions.explanation: Plastic is strong and waterproof, making it best for a water bucket. Glass breaks, paper tears, and cloth leaks.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose glass because it holds water, but it breaks easily.

questions.stem: Go outside and collect three different materials (e.g., a leaf, a stone, a piece of plastic). Show them to your teacher and name them.

criteria.description: Collects three items from the environment
Correctly names the material of each item

questions.explanation: This tests real-world observation and naming of materials.

questions.stem: Which statement about materials is TRUE?
options: Materials can only be found in shops
Different materials have different properties and uses
Materials are only made by humans
questions.explanation: Materials have different properties (hard, soft, transparent) which makes them useful for different things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all materials can be used for the same purposes.

questions.stem: Why would you NOT use paper to make a cup for drinking water?

criteria.description: States that paper gets wet and tears
States that water will leak out

hints: What happens to paper when it touches water?
questions.explanation: Paper is not waterproof; it gets soft and tears when it gets wet, so water would leak out.
